newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson asks for new wrongful death trial.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson asks for new wrongful death trial.

text.p: O.J. Simpson on Friday asked the judge in his civil wrongful death lawsuit to order a retrial in the hope of reversing a jury verdict finding him liable for the deaths of his ex-wife and her friend.

Simpson, who was found not guilty in criminal court in 1995 of the double murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman, was found responsible for their deaths by a civil court jury in Santa Monica in February after being sued by the families of the victims.
Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman were stabbed and slashed to death outside Simpson's ex-wife's condominium in June 1994.

In court papers filed on Friday, Dan Leonard, Simpson's lawyer, argued that even if Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki turned down the request for a new trial, the former football star should not have to pay $25 million in punitive damages to the plaintiffs.

"In this case the jury awarded punitive damages which ... amount to more than 300 percent of even the plaintiffs' grossly inflated version of Simpson's net worth. Obviously, this does not pass muster under California law," Leonard said in his court papers.

Simpson was ordered to pay punitive damages of $12.5 million each to the estate of his ex-wife, whose heirs are his two young children, Justin and Sydney, and to Goldman's natural parents, Fred Goldman and Sharon Rufo, who are divorced.
In addition, the former running back for the Buffalo Bills of the National Football League was ordered to pay Goldman $7 million and Rufo $1.5 million in actual damages.
Leonard, in his court motion on Friday, alleged that the jury pool was tainted and was not representative of the black community, Simpson being an African-American.

"Initially, the jury pool started out with 35 percent African-Americans. Nonetheless, the final jury panel ended up with no jurors of African-American descent, excluding a single individual who was both half African-American and half Asian," Leonard argued in his filing.
The civil court jury voted 12-0 in finding Simpson liable for the deaths after a four-month trial, although under California law only a 9-3 verdict was necessary for a finding of unlawful death.

Simpson's lawyers also argued that Fujisaki made a number of judicial errors in conducting the civil trial, including allowing evidence of previous domestic violence by Simpson against his ex-wife, permitting Nicole Brown Simpson's diaries to be read to the jury, and allowing testimony about his allegedly failing a lie detector test after the murders.
Fujisaki has set hearings on Leonard's motions for April 22 and April 25.
